audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding fixed-strict, initial (initial stress), word domain rests on Blake 1979:25-26, the reference grammar and terminal description of a dormant language; the quotation is verbatim in the open-access PDF we hold at the stated pages, and the passage itself retracts the 1969 morpheme-initial/alternating account that StressTyp2 encoded, so the recorded contradiction with the database is also substantiated. No better source exists or is listed in Glottolog (no phonology-typed works; no instrumental study possible). The only defect is bookkeeping: the record's quote/cite/loc/grade fields are blank while the verified quotation sits in the domain quotation/the domain locator -- promote Blake 1979:25-26 into the primary evidence fields with a top strength of the evidence. no reclassification.

sources.quote: Stress is realised primarily in terms of loudness as in English. [...] Each word is marked by primary stress on the first syllable. I'm not sure that there are any other rules for stress within words. I previously reported (Blake 1969:16-17) that the first syllable of every polysyllabic morpheme received stress and that sequences of more than two unstressed syllables did not occur. I now believe that there is only one phonological rule and that this rule places primary stress on the first syllable of the word. Other secondary stresses may occur but their appearance seems to be sporadic, being determined by tempo and by hesitations and the like. It would be unusual for a secondary stress to fall on a syllable other than the first syllable of a non-word-initial polysyllabic morpheme where such a morpheme occurs [...] In general secondary stresses occur spaced by one or two unstressed syllables but in fluent speech they hardly occur at all and I'm inclined to think that their occurrence is determined by some natural iambic tendency towards alternating stressed and unstressed syllables rather than as the result of the application of a rule. sources.locator: Sections 2.17 Stress and 2.17.1 Word Stress, printed pp. 25-26
sources.note: Primary stress fixed on the first syllable of every word, the only stress rule; matches the catalog initial stress (initial, no rule-governed secondary). Secondary stress: sporadic, tempo/hesitation-driven, not a rule; when present it falls on the first syllable of a non-word-initial polysyllabic morpheme, spaced by one or two unstressed syllables (author calls this an 'iambic tendency' toward alternation). sources.note: Syntax paper on noun-phrase structure, pronoun-determiners and clitics; the only occurrence of 'stress' is a discourse-pragmatic remark that general words (which become clitics) carry given information and are unstressed. No statement of Kalkatungu word stress, no rule, no secondary stress, weight, domain or exceptions; tone not mentioned. Nothing bears on the catalog fixed: initial syllable rule, which the catalog cites from Blake 1979.
